title: Chapter 64 – The Veil Re-Spun
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The straw dummy on the threshing floor has no face, and by the second week of winter Jian has begun to hate it.

It is a bundle of rice straw bound over a pine post, with a plank for a chest and a rusted pot lid for a heart. Hu built it in an afternoon, with a grunt and a pair of shears. It stands in the middle of the floor under a sky the color of wet slate, and every night Jian stands thirty paces from it with his hands at his sides and tries to hit the lid.

Seam Needle, he thinks, and lets it go.

The Qi leaves his fingertips as a thread of cold, thin and bright, and crosses the floor faster than a man can follow. It does not strike the lid. It passes through the plank behind it, through the post, through the stacked firewood at the back of the shed, and he hears a soft crack from somewhere in the dark, where a roof beam has just been given a hole the width of a barley stalk.

He lowers his hand.

Too much, he thinks. Again.

It is the same every night. Before the Bloom, a Seam Needle was a careful, expensive thing, a thread he spun out of his own thin reserve and aimed with all his attention at a seam in a body. Now the Seal sits in his dantian like a small slow wheel, turning through its four seasons, and everything he draws from it comes out purer, heavier, and nearly thirty percent stronger than he asks. He wants a scratch. The Needle gives him a lance.

The power is not the problem. The power is a gift, and he knows precisely what it cost. The problem is that a spell he cannot measure is a spell he cannot trust, and a man who throws too much at a target spends too much of himself, and a boy at the Outer Court who punches holes through walls will be asked why.

Less, he thinks, and breathes out. He lets half the Qi leak away into the dark before it reaches his hand, on purpose, a little wasted cold that falls on the frozen ground like breath. The Needle that follows is smaller, and slower, and it taps the pot lid with a sound like a pin on a bell.

There.

He tries again. The lid rings. Again, and it does not. He misses by a hair, and the Needle goes into the straw, and the straw takes it, and a thin curl of smoke rises off the dummy's shoulder.

Eleven, he thinks. Eleven hits in twenty.

It is a better count than the first night, which was three. He wipes his nose with the back of his hand. It comes away dark.

You are bleeding, says Pebble.

She is perched on the wall above the floor, small and round against the pale sky, with her paws tucked under her chin. She has grown a little in the winter, an inch of new scale at the base of the tail, a slow patient shine returning to the old ones. She has not spoken in words, of course. She speaks as she always has, by the pressure of a thought against his own, like a hand laid on the back of the neck.

A little.

It is the Seal. It pulls on the small vessels when you hold it back.

Is that your opinion, or something you know?

It is my opinion. A pause. But I am usually right about vessels.

He does not smile, quite. He puts a pinch of snow to his lip, and tilts his head, and looks at the lid.

The dark does not give anything back. It is a still, cold, ordinary night on a hill that has lost forty of its own and four hundred of its enemies and does not yet know what to do with the silence. Somewhere behind him, in the long low shape of the forge, a single window is lit. His mother's.

Again, he thinks.

* * *

She starts him on the Veil in the loft above the granary, on the third morning after the new moon, in the half-dark before the guards change.

"Sit," says Qinghe.

He sits. She sits across from him on a sack of seed barley, with her knees drawn up and her hands loose, and for a while she does nothing at all except look at him. It is a look he has learned to read. It is not the look of a mother. It is the look of a woman who walked a road alone for twelve years and learned to value what a person does with their face when they think no one is judging.

"Your old Veil was a still pond," she says. "Hold one layer. Hold another. Sit very quiet, and let anyone who looks think there is nothing to see. It was a good Veil for a boy of seven. It broke because a Bloom is not still."

"Yes."

"The Seal moves. It turns. It cannot sit in one place, and if you force it, it forces you." She lifts one hand and turns it palm upward, slowly. "So we do not hide it. We give it a face. A face that moves the same way a living body moves."

She shows him.

It is not a technique he has met before. It is a way of holding the Qi: not pressing it down, but letting it run along a set course, a kind of lazy circle, a slow shallow wheel set inside the true one. The wheel turns the way a season turns. It swells in the spring and thins in the summer and is quiet in the autumn, and when it reaches winter it nearly stops, and then, very softly, begins again.

"A person who watches a man for a minute sees a man," says Qinghe. "A person who watches him for a day sees a rhythm. If the rhythm is strange, they will notice. If the rhythm is ordinary, they will see an ordinary man whose Qi breathes the way Qi breathes." She taps her own sternum. "Everyone's does. Even mine. Even yours, though you have never looked. The trick is to look first, and give them something to find that you chose."

He closes his eyes. He reaches inward, past the straight cold line of the Needle and the thick bright knot of the Bloom, down to the small slow wheel, and begins, clumsily, to lay a second one over it.

It takes him the rest of the morning to hold it for ten breaths.

This is a Veil, he thinks. Not a wall. A mask that moves.

By noon he can hold it for a hundred. By evening, as the light goes, for a full quarter hour, and the false wheel is turning cleanly on its false course, spring to summer, summer to autumn, and the real one is sunk beneath it, still and dark and deep. When Qinghe opens her own sense toward him, he feels her touch pass over the false wheel, pause, and slide on, as a hand slides over a smooth stone.

"Three layers," she says. "You read as a boy at the third layer of Qi Refining, who is a little tired and has a good teacher. If I did not know, I would have said so."

"What does it cost?"

"You tell me."

He thinks. It is not a trick. His recovery is slower, he realizes. It is not a great deal; it is like walking with a stone in one shoe. When he drops the Veil and lets his reserve fill, the Qi comes back in a trickle, not a stream.

"A fifth," he says. "More or less. While it is up, I recover a fifth less."

"A fifth." She nods. "It is not nothing. It is also the cheapest mask I know. The expensive ones are the ones that hide you completely, and a man who hides completely is a man someone wants to look at." She gets to her feet, brushing seed-dust from her knees. "Do it again tomorrow. And the day after. You will need it for as long as you are in that place."

He opens his mouth to say something about how it is only a Veil.

"It is not only a Veil," she says, before he can. "It is the first thing they will see."

* * *

She asks him on the fourth evening.

They are in the granary, at the long bench by the cold forge, because Hu has gone to the village for oil and Wenyuan is closeted with Wenjun and the quarterly figures. A single lamp is lit between them. Qinghe has laid out a cloth, a bowl of water, and a row of small slender needles, as if she meant to teach him acupuncture, which she does not. It is only that she has found her hands are steadier when she has something to hold.

"I said I would ask one thing," she says. "In the autumn. I said it would be a true question, and that you would give me a true answer."

"You did."

"I have not asked."

"No."

"I have been waiting." She does not look up from the needle. "Not because I did not know what to ask. Because I wanted to be sure that I could bear the answer."

Jian waits.

She puts the needle down.

"Are you afraid," she says, "of what you are becoming?"

It is not the question he expected. He had braced for something sharp, something with a blade in it: what is in the Garden, what is in your head, where do you go in the dark. He had planned three lies and one half-truth. None of them fit.

He sits in the lamplight with his hands on his knees and looks at her. She is forty, or a little more. She has gray in her braid that was not there a year ago. She has her own father's trick of keeping very still when she is hurting.

Tell the truth, he thinks. Or something that is made of it.

"Yes," he says.

She does not move.

"Not of the killing," he says slowly. "I thought that would be the thing. I thought, when I had to, I would be sick, and I would not sleep, and it would break something. It did not. It was..." He searches for the word, and finds that it is not a kind one. "It was arithmetic. They were in the way of a thing I had to keep, and I removed them. And afterward I counted the graves, and the numbers came out right, and I was sorry, and I was also calm." His voice is very level. "It is the calm I am afraid of. I think that if I were a better person I would not be able to do the sum so easily."

The lamp ticks.

"I do not want to become a man who can," he says. "And I do not know how to stop."

For a time she says nothing at all. Then she gets up from her stool and comes round the bench, and does not embrace him, because she has never been quick to, but sits beside him and puts her shoulder against his, so that they lean on each other like two stones in a wall.

"I was afraid of it too," says Qinghe. "At nineteen. On the Salt Road. I killed a man who had a wife, and I knew he had a wife, and I did the sum." She lets out a breath. "I stayed afraid of it for ten years. I think it is the only thing that kept me from turning into the thing I was fighting. A man who is not afraid of his own calm is not calm. He is cold."

"What did you do?"

"I counted them, as you do." Her voice is dry. "And then I wrote their names on a strip of paper, and burned it, once a year, on the day. It is a very small thing. It did not make me good. It made me aware." She turns her head and looks at him. "Keep your ledger, Jian. Keep it as you keep the other. The day it stops costing you anything is the day you should be afraid."

It is not comfort. It is something better. It is a rule, and it is hers, and he writes it down in his head beside the others.

"Thank you," he says.

"Do not thank me." She stands. "Go and practice the Veil. And Jian."

"Yes?"

"Eat something."

* * *

Pebble will not be put away.

It is not a quarrel, because she has no way to quarrel. It is a quality of her silence. He has taken Ke Tian's pouch from under his tunic that night, in the forge, with the door barred, and has laid it open on the bench and tried to explain, in the gentlest thoughts he can manage, that when they go to the Outer Court there will be a Beast Hall, and a scan, and a registrar who counts the creatures of every disciple.

I know about the Hall, she says.

They will see you.

I know.

Then I must find a way to put you somewhere they cannot. He turns the pouch over in his hands. It is a good pouch, a Yellow, a little over two cubic meters of dead gray space. It has already swallowed the cradle without complaint. Not for long. Only until they have counted.

I will not go in the gray bag.

It would not hold you.

He means it as a comfort. He knows, as every child at the Ford knows, that no pouch will take anything that breathes. It refuses flatly, the way a cup refuses a stone, and a creature pushed against its mouth is shoved out again, frightened and unharmed. There is a reason the other kind of bag exists, and a reason they cost forty stones, and a reason the shops that sell them stand at the far end of the market, where the smell of animal does not trouble the jade and the paper.

I know, says Pebble, very small. I was only saying.

He puts the pouch down. He looks at her. She is sitting on the bench with her forepaws together and her face turned toward the dark corner of the forge, and she is not looking at him at all.

Pebble?

There is a door.

He holds still.

It is not here, she says. It is in the place where I was before. I remember it only when someone tells me I will be put somewhere. I do not remember what is behind. Only a hand. A flicker, a pale light at the back of his thoughts, like a lamp seen through a curtain: a heavy round door, a bronze rim, and a hand laid flat against it. A big hand, with a scar across the knuckles. And a voice. It says, stay until the gardener comes.

The flicker goes out.

He sits very still. In the forge, the coals tick. Outside, a long way off, a dog barks twice and stops.

I do not know whose voice, says Pebble. I do not think it was cruel. A pause. But I did not like to be shut.

Then you will not be shut, he says. I promise. A bag for the Hall. Only for the Hall. And I will open it myself.

All right.

She climbs into his lap. She is warm, and heavier than she was, and her new scale is a bright small coin against the dull ones. He puts his hand on her back, and they sit for a long time in the sound of the coals, not saying anything, while the gray pouch lies open on the bench like a mouth that has nothing to eat.

Gardener, he thinks. It said gardener.

He has not told her what the panel said, in the autumn, when she touched the heart plate. He has not needed to. He has understood, in a way he could not have explained to Hu or to his mother or to anyone in the world, that she was not the key. She was the one who had been left to wait.

* * *

Lin Yue finds him on the forge steps, two days before the deputy, with a rice cake in each hand.

She is eight and a half. She has no root. It is a fact the clan has stopped saying aloud, the way a family stops mentioning a crooked tooth, and she has taken the silence as a kind of license to look at everything and say what she sees. She hands him a rice cake without asking, sits down beside him, and eats her own with great attention.

"You are different," she says.

"I am the same."

"You are like a candle somebody blew on." She licks sugar off her thumb. "Before, you were a candle that was just a candle. Now you are one that goes a little small, and a little big, and a little small. Like it is breathing."

He sits very still, with the rice cake halfway to his mouth.

"It is not that," says Lin Yue, "that it is wrong. It is only that it is slow. Real candles do not go slow." She frowns at the quarry. "Grandfather's did. When he was sick."

She cannot feel Qi, he thinks. She has no root. She cannot see a wheel, or a layer, or a seam.

She can see a rhythm, says Pebble, from his shoulder, with distant interest. Anyone can. They only do not look.

"It is a game," he says, carefully. "Mother is teaching me to keep still."

"Is it a good game?"

"It is a hard one."

"Then you should win it," says Lin Yue, with the serene authority of the very young, and eats the last of her cake. She is quiet for a while. "Will you write to me? From the Court?"

"Every month."

"Real letters. Not the kind Father writes, with all the numbers."

"With no numbers at all."

"One number," she says. "How many people were nice to you." She gets up, brushes the crumbs from her lap, and goes back into the house, and does not look round.

He sits on the steps a long time with the rice cake in his hand.

A Veil can fool a deputy, he thinks. It cannot fool a child who loves me.

It is not a thing he can fix. He does not think he wants to.

* * *

The deputy comes back at midwinter, for the quarter survey.

He comes with the same five clerks, the same two guards, the same wooden tally-stick at his belt. It is a bright, bitter morning with ice on the quarry road, and the Lin clan has turned out in its winter cloaks to stand along the gate in the second hour of the day. It is a courtesy. It is also, Jian understands, a message: we have nothing to hide, and here are all our faces.

He stands in the third row, between Lin Hu and a girl called Rui who sells pickles, with his hands folded and his eyes lowered.

The Seasons Veil is up. He feels it turn in him, slow, shallow, a little tilted toward the first of the spring. He has been holding it since dawn, and the cost is a steady, small ache behind the eyes, like a bruise he cannot stop pressing. His recovery is down by a fifth. He has already counted how many breaths of Seam Needle that leaves him, and it is not enough, and he has put the number away.

Deputy Dou walks the line.

He does it slowly. He is not a man who hurries. He walks along the Lin gate with his stick under his arm and his chin a little down, as a man walks a row of fence posts, and he looks at each face, and at each hand, and at each pair of shoes, with the same patient, exhausted attention. There is no malice in it. There is no kindness either. He pauses at Wenshi, and at Aunt Wenjun, and at the schoolmaster, who gives him a sharp small nod.

He reaches the third row.

Early Foundation, thinks Jian, with a distant, cold interest. He has not been able to tell before. It is in the way the man's steps fall, a quarter-beat too even, the sign of a body that has been rebuilt from the bones out. The Garden Office sends an early Foundation as a deputy. They are not taking this lightly.

Dou stops.

He stops in front of Lin Hu, who is twelve and has been told to stand very straight and is trying, and he looks down at the boy for a moment. Then he turns his head, a single degree, to the left.

Jian does not breathe.

The man's eyes are a pale, tired brown. They move across Jian's face, and his folded hands, and the small plain knot of cord at his belt, and they do not stop. They do not narrow, or sharpen, or turn inward in the way that an eye turns when it has found a thing and is thinking about it. They simply pass, as they have passed over the others, and rest for the briefest instant on the girl beside him, and move on.

And behind him, in the fold of the second wheel, the real one turns quietly in its dark.

It is not until the deputy has reached the end of the line, and the clerks have gone in with their boards, and the clan has begun, in small relieved clusters, to drift apart, that Jian lets himself breathe out. His knees feel strange. He has been holding the Veil for six hours, and when he lets it drop, a long gray weariness comes down over him, like a wet cloak.

"You did well," says a voice at his shoulder.

He turns.

Qinghe is standing behind him, with her hands tucked into her sleeves and her face quite blank. She has not looked at him once during the whole inspection. She is looking at the gate now, where the deputy's gray figure is bending over a clerk's board, making a note.

"It held," says Jian.

"It held." She does not turn. "He is early Foundation. He did not see it. That is good, and it is a good Veil, and I am glad of you." A pause. "Listen to me."

"Yes."

"It hides what you are," says Qinghe, very low. "It does not hide what you do. If a man sees you cast a spell your face should not be able to cast, if a man sees you walk where a boy of three layers could not, if a man watches you for a day and a night and sees the weight you carry, the Veil is only paint on a wall. They will not look for a boy at the third layer. They will look for the one who does what you do." She finally turns her head, and her eyes are quiet and steady and a great deal older than her face. "So do nothing for them to see."

He nods. He cannot find anything to say.

"Go and sit down," says his mother. "You are the color of candle wax."

She walks away across the frozen yard, a straight narrow figure in a gray cloak, with her hands still in her sleeves, and does not look back. Jian stands a moment longer, in the thin winter sun, listening to the sound of a clerk's pen scratch on a board.

Somewhere deep in his sleeve, in the gray dead space of a stolen pouch, a small cold coil gives one slow pulse, like a sleeper turning in a dream, and goes still.
